newsitem.title: USA: American Air dismisses pilots' offer as strike looms.
newsitem.headline: American Air dismisses pilots' offer as strike looms.

text.p: American Airlines dismissed on Thursday the latest offer from its pilots aimed at averting a strike, and the chairman of the nation's second-largest carrier called for binding arbitration in the bitter dispute.

A key issue in the dispute is whether American Airlines can fly the small jets of its regional carrier, American Eagle, with lower-paid pilots belonging to another union, a move opposed by the Allied Pilots Association.
The airline, a unit of AMR Corp., says it needs the low-cost operation to be competitive with other major airlines flying commuter services.

In a bid to compromise, the pilots' union said late on Wednesday it would be willing to allow union pilots to fly regional jets at lower pay as a step toward reaching a new contract and avoiding a strike on Friday night.
But a spokesman for American dismissed the offer, saying, "It was a bunch of verbiage on paper."
Separately, American Airlines Chairman Robert Crandall called for binding government arbitration of the dispute, a proposal the pilots had previously rejected.
"I think mandatory binding arbitration should be required" to prevent airline strikes, Crandall told a congressional subcommittee.
The two sides were already negotiating in Washington with a federal mediator present but binding arbitration would increase the government role.
Crandall told a hearing of a House Transportation subcommittee that he was unsure if a strike could be avoided.
"We have two choices: we can either cave in or take a strike," he said. "A strike of 90 days will destroy this airline."
The pilots' union has pledged to strike after midnight Friday (0500 GMT Saturday) if no new contract is reached.
A strike against American would throw the nation's transport system into chaos. In preparation, American cancelled almost all its Friday night international flights.
As the talks entered their fourth day of non-stop bargaining, President Bill Clinton was keeping a close watch.

Clinton could intervene and name an emergency board to try to resolve the issues. Creation of a board would prevent any work stoppages for 60 days while the board and the two parties tried again to end their differences.

The impact of a potential strike was already being felt where American has a major presence, with travel agents steering passengers away from the airline and American trying to rebook passengers on other carriers.
Areas particularly hard hit would be the Caribbean, now at the height of its winter tourist season, and the Colorado Rockies, a popular destination for skiers.
American scrapped 129 international flights scheduled to leave on Friday. The only flights that were to go ahead were 14 to London. Return flights on Saturday were also cancelled.

The carrier said it would reschedule its international passengers to Europe, the Far East and Latin America on earlier American flights or on other airlines. But travel agents said there likely would not be enough seats on other carriers to handle all the stranded American passengers.
